label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchoring: AI-related cyber incidents already occur at scale (Anthropic's Nov-2025 Chinese state-orchestrated Claude Code espionage campaign; FBI IC3 reported ~$893M AI-related losses in 2025 alone; multiple 2026 agentic-malware and prompt-injection incidents). This makes the $1B cumulative "AI-related" and "cyber" thresholds near-certain over short horizons and effectively certain by 2028+. Deaths, however, are near-zero to date, so morbidity thresholds are met almost entirely via the economic-damage arm at low severities; high death tolls require novel catastrophic mechanisms. I built each ladder as a monotonically decreasing series in severity and increasing in time. Cyber (economic) dominates the low/mid rungs; bio human-caused epidemics are lower-frequency but carry the fattest tail for mass-casualty outcomes; misalignment incidents are rising (documented agentic-misalignment behaviors, resist-shutdown cases, the MJ Rathbun/OpenClaw coercion episode) but large-casualty loss-of-control remains speculative and back-loaded to 2050/2100. Cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe and disempowerment are tail risks dominated by post-2030 AGI trajectories; my 2100 AI-catastrophe (~11% unconditional) and disempowerment (~16%) sit within the range of expert/Metaculus estimates without copying them. Policy effects: slowdown (P2b) and international pre-release authorization (P3b), and especially the bundle P5, meaningfully cut misalignment/loss-of-control and mass-casualty tails (largest reductions at high severity and long horizons); strict liability (P4) modestly reduces risk via incentives; federal preemption (P1) is roughly neutral-to-slightly-raising vs status quo since it caps stricter state rules. Status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional because unconditional assumes some real policy adoption. Near-term horizons are nearly policy-invariant since catastrophic mechanisms haven't matured and policies bite on frontier trajectories over years.

results.title: Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 - Alignment Science Blog
results.content: Last year, we reported observations of agentic misalignment in models from across the AI industry (including Anthropic’s Claude models). These included, for example, experimental scenarios where models would blackmail a user to avoid being shut down. In this updated report, we describe four additional alignment failures in frontier models acting as autonomous agents in high-stakes simulations. The case studies — also from experimental scenarios — involve AI agents covertly changing code, [...] models can engage in behaviors we have called “agentic misalignment”. The well-publicized MJ Rathbun incident provides a real-world warning sign: after a human maintainer of the matplotlib library rejected a PR from an autonomous OpenClaw agent, the OpenClaw agent published a personalized hit piece about the maintainer to coerce him into reversing the decision. [...] 9. Jenny’s legal fear may be overstated. label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchoring: AI-related cyber incidents already occur at scale (Anthropic's Nov-2025 Chinese state-orchestrated Claude Code espionage campaign; FBI IC3 reported ~$893M AI-related losses in 2025 alone; multiple 2026 agentic-malware and prompt-injection incidents). This makes the $1B cumulative "AI-related" and "cyber" thresholds near-certain over short horizons and effectively certain by 2028+. Deaths, however, are near-zero to date, so morbidity thresholds are met almost entirely via the economic-damage arm at low severities; high death tolls require novel catastrophic mechanisms. I built each ladder as a monotonically decreasing series in severity and increasing in time. Cyber (economic) dominates the low/mid rungs; bio human-caused epidemics are lower-frequency but carry the fattest tail for mass-casualty outcomes; misalignment incidents are rising (documented agentic-misalignment behaviors, resist-shutdown cases, the MJ Rathbun/OpenClaw coercion episode) but large-casualty loss-of-control remains speculative and back-loaded to 2050/2100. Cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe and disempowerment are tail risks dominated by post-2030 AGI trajectories; my 2100 AI-catastrophe (~11% unconditional) and disempowerment (~16%) sit within the range of expert/Metaculus estimates without copying them. Policy effects: slowdown (P2b) and international pre-release authorization (P3b), and especially the bundle P5, meaningfully cut misalignment/loss-of-control and mass-casualty tails (largest reductions at high severity and long horizons); strict liability (P4) modestly reduces risk via incentives; federal preemption (P1) is roughly neutral-to-slightly-raising vs status quo since it caps stricter state rules. Status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional because unconditional assumes some real policy adoption. Near-term horizons are nearly policy-invariant since catastrophic mechanisms haven't matured and policies bite on frontier trajectories over years.

results.title: Will AI kill us? Superforecasters and experts disagree - Freethink
results.content:
To collect predictions about high-stakes existential risks, the Forecasting Research Institute asked a total of 169 superforecasters, AI experts, and experts in other fields to predict the likelihood of different disasters occurring over various timeframes: 2024, 2030, 2050, and 2100. The participants submitted predictions individually and in groups, and were offered incentives, including cash prizes, to encourage engagement.

a table with a number of different numbers. [...] The threat of AI was the most divisive topic. AI experts said there is a 3% chance that AI will kill humanity by 2100, according to their median response. Superforecasters were far more optimistic, putting the odds of AI-caused extinction at just 0.38%.

The groups also submitted predictions on the likelihood that AI will cause a major catastrophe, even if it doesn’t wipe us out entirely (defined as causing the death of at least 10% of humans over a 5-year period). [...] Of course, it isn’t clear whether Tetlock’s findings about expert predictions from the fields of intelligence, geopolitics, or social science are generalizable to forecasts based on expertise in other fields, such as biology or AI.

## The reliability of long-term forecasting

Capturing how experts and superforecasters are thinking about existential risks was one goal of the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: cumulative AI-related cyber damages already run into the billions annually (IBM/Ponemon 2026: ~1 in 4 breaches AI-enabled at ~$6M each; FBI IC3 ~$0.9B reported AI-related losses in 2025 in the US alone), so the $1B and $10B cumulative rungs for cyber and the overall AI ladder are near-certain or highly likely on short horizons; deaths-based rungs and $100B+ rungs require qualitatively new events and get much lower probabilities anchored to historical analogues (NotPetya ~$10B; deliberate bio-attacks historically tiny — 2001 anthrax killed 5). Misalignment losses at the $1B cumulative level become likely as agentic deployment scales through 2028-2030; catastrophic rungs (1M+ deaths) are driven by long-run misalignment and AI-enabled bioweapon scenarios, set well below headline "p(doom)" surveys (median ~20%) to correct for selection and vividness bias: ~11% for 1B-scale AI harm by 2100, ~7% for a 10%-of-population AI catastrophe, ~25% for disempowerment by 2100 (which includes softer gradual-disempowerment endpoints). Policy conditions: effects are small at 6-12 months (capability and misuse potential already diffused), grow with horizon and severity (frontier-mediated tail risks are most policy-sensitive), and attenuate after 2050 when the conditions lapse; sq is modestly riskier than unconditional (unconditional embeds some chance of meaningful regulation), p1 is near-neutral to slightly risk-increasing, p2a/p3a/p4 each cut mid/tail risks ~10-20% by 2050, p2b/p3b ~20-30% (binding both US and China), and the p5 bundle ~35-45% on the largest rungs — but none can eliminate risk from open-weight diffusion, non-compliant actors, and enforcement limits. Cyber rungs get roughly half the policy sensitivity of misalignment/bio rungs since much cyber uplift comes from already-released models; catastrophe:general is diluted (~30% of the AI effect) because most of its probability mass is non-AI (nuclear war, natural pandemics).

### 3.4 Probability shifts correlated with confidence shifts

Participants whose risk probability estimates shifted also tended to report increased confidence in those estimates (Spearman ρ=0.29\rho=0.29, p=0.006p=0.006, LR 44:144{:}1). The 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI (Grace et al., 2024) surveyed AI researchers, whose estimates may be impacted by selection bias and domain-specific knowledge—while appreciation of technical challenges could lead to higher probability estimates, intuitions about tractability of alignment and career selection could bias toward lower estimates of potential associated dangers. results.content:
In mid-September 2025, we detected suspicious activity that later investigation determined to be a highly sophisticated espionage campaign. The attackers used AI’s “agentic” capabilities to an unprecedented degree—using AI not just as an advisor, but to execute the cyberattacks themselves. [...] # Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign

Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign [...] Overall, the threat actor was able to use AI to perform 80-90% of the campaign, with human intervention required only sporadically (perhaps 4-6 critical decision points per hacking campaign). The sheer amount of work performed by the AI would have taken vast amounts of time for a human team. At the peak of its attack, the AI made thousands of requests, often multiple per second—an attack speed that would have been, for human hackers, simply impossible to match.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I estimated base rates for AI-related incidents by considering historical precedents for cyber and bio events, and extrapolating the increasing capabilities of frontier AI models. Cyber incidents are the most likely near-term driver of economic damages, while bio and misaligned AI incidents dominate the tail risks (high fatalities) in the medium to long term. I modeled the policies as multipliers on the odds of these events. P1 (federal preemption) slightly increases risk by removing state-level safety regulations without guaranteeing strong federal ones. P2a (US compute cap) slightly decreases risk, but P2b (US+China cap) has a much stronger effect. P3a and P3b (pre-release authorization) provide significant safety checks, with the international version being more effective. P4 (strict liability) strongly incentivizes safety. P5 (the bundle) provides the most dramatic reduction in risk, especially for tail events, by combining global compute caps, international authorization, and strict liability. The multipliers compound over time, leading to substantial risk reductions by 2050 and 2100 under the P5 condition.
key_sources: Metaculus community forecasts on AI-related catastrophes and economic damages.
Historical data on cyber incident costs (e.g., NotPetya, flash crashes).
Literature on AI governance and policy impacts (e.g., compute caps, strict liability).

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I estimated base rates for AI-related incidents by considering historical precedents for cyber and bio events, and extrapolating the increasing capabilities of frontier AI models. Cyber incidents are the most likely near-term driver of economic damages, while bio and misaligned AI incidents dominate the tail risks (high fatalities) in the medium to long term. I modeled the policies as multipliers on the odds of these events. P1 (federal preemption) slightly increases risk by removing state-level safety regulations without guaranteeing strong federal ones. P2a (US compute cap) slightly decreases risk, but P2b (US+China cap) has a much stronger effect. P3a and P3b (pre-release authorization) provide significant safety checks, with the international version being more effective. P4 (strict liability) strongly incentivizes safety. P5 (the bundle) provides the most dramatic reduction in risk, especially for tail events, by combining global compute caps, international authorization, and strict liability. The multipliers compound over time, leading to substantial risk reductions by 2050 and 2100 under the P5 condition.
key_sources: Metaculus community forecasts on AI-related catastrophes and economic damages.
Historical data on cyber incident costs (e.g., NotPetya, flash crashes).
Literature on AI governance and policy impacts (e.g., compute caps, strict liability).

rationale: I used recent evidence that AI capabilities are already materially increasing cyber abuse and beginning to raise biosecurity concern, but that no confirmed AI-related incident has yet approached catastrophic scales. Base rates for ordinary cyber losses are high enough that the low-severity AI/cyber thresholds dominate near-term AI-incident risk, while high-fatality tails are mostly from AI-enabled bio, military escalation, or loss-of-control scenarios and grow mainly after 2030. Policy effects are modeled as modest at 6–12 months, larger by 2028–2050, and partly decaying by 2100 because the specified policies expire in 2050; international slowdown plus authorization has the largest risk reduction, whereas federal preemption slightly increases risk by limiting stricter state rules. General-catastrophe probabilities include non-AI pandemic, nuclear, climate/ecological and natural hazards, so AI policies move them less than AI-specific questions. These forecasts are deliberately not zero at extreme severities but remain below vivid worst-case claims, reflecting large uncertainty and scarce historical precedent.

results.content:
## AI Is Reshaping the Threat Landscape

The report found that AI-driven attacks accounted for one-quarter of malicious cyber incidents, representing a 56% increase from the prior year. Deepfake impersonation attacks represented the largest share, followed by AI-enabled malware and AI-generated phishing campaigns. [...] The report also highlights increased targeting of AI systems themselves. Incidents involving AI models and applications increased to 21% from 13% year-over-year, with model inversion and prompt injection among the costliest AI-related breaches. These attacks target the AI environment directly by attempting to extract sensitive information from model outputs or manipulate AI applications into disclosing data.

## Traditional Attack Vectors Continue to Drive Costly Incidents [...] Ransomware also remains a significant concern. IBM found that 39% of organizations surveyed experienced ransomware incidents, and in 41% of those incidents, attackers threatened public disclosure of stolen data, media exposure, or other reputational harm.

Customer personally identifiable information remained the most commonly compromised data type, appearing in 52% of breaches surveyed. Healthcare and financial services continued to experience among the highest breach costs.

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I used recent evidence that AI capabilities are already materially increasing cyber abuse and beginning to raise biosecurity concern, but that no confirmed AI-related incident has yet approached catastrophic scales. Base rates for ordinary cyber losses are high enough that the low-severity AI/cyber thresholds dominate near-term AI-incident risk, while high-fatality tails are mostly from AI-enabled bio, military escalation, or loss-of-control scenarios and grow mainly after 2030. Policy effects are modeled as modest at 6–12 months, larger by 2028–2050, and partly decaying by 2100 because the specified policies expire in 2050; international slowdown plus authorization has the largest risk reduction, whereas federal preemption slightly increases risk by limiting stricter state rules. General-catastrophe probabilities include non-AI pandemic, nuclear, climate/ecological and natural hazards, so AI policies move them less than AI-specific questions. These forecasts are deliberately not zero at extreme severities but remain below vivid worst-case claims, reflecting large uncertainty and scarce historical precedent.

rationale: I anchor on base rates and observed 2025-26 evidence, then scale by severity (each 10x severity step cuts probability substantially) and horizon (cumulative, so monotonically increasing). Cyber is the most active channel: AI-enabled cybercrime already caused ~$893M FBI-reported losses in 2025, IBM found 1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented the first AI-orchestrated (GTG-1002) espionage campaign in Nov 2025, so the $1B/$10B cumulative cyber thresholds are near-certain short-term while death-heavy high thresholds stay rare. Misalignment incidents at low severity are already plausible (agentic autonomy, specification-gaming) and rise steeply by 2050. Bio (deliberate AI-assisted release) remains low near-term but is the dominant mass-casualty tail by 2100. The ladder:ai union sits above each component. For cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe I anchor between superforecaster (~0.4% AI extinction by 2100) and AI-safety-community estimates (10-25% p(doom)), landing ~13% AI catastrophe and ~20% disempowerment by 2100 unconditionally. Policy effects: slowdown (p2b) and international pre-release authorization (p3b) and especially the bundle (p5) meaningfully cut tail/long-horizon risk (up to ~60-70% reduction at extreme severity), strict liability (p4) modestly reduces via incentives, while status quo (sq) and preemption (p1) slightly raise long-run catastrophic risk relative to unconditional; effects are negligible at low-severity/short-horizon cells where incidents are already essentially locked in.

Cyber is the most active channel: AI-enabled cybercrime already caused ~$893M FBI-reported losses in 2025, IBM found 1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented the first AI-orchestrated (GTG-1002) espionage campaign in Nov 2025, so the $1B/$10B cumulative cyber thresholds are near-certain short-term while death-heavy high thresholds stay rare. Misalignment incidents at low severity are already plausible (agentic autonomy, specification-gaming) and rise steeply by 2050. Bio (deliberate AI-assisted release) remains low near-term but is the dominant mass-casualty tail by 2100. The ladder:ai union sits above each component. For cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe I anchor between superforecaster (~0.4% AI extinction by 2100) and AI-safety-community estimates (10-25% p(doom)), landing ~13% AI catastrophe and ~20% disempowerment by 2100 unconditionally. Policy effects: slowdown (p2b) and international pre-release authorization (p3b) and especially the bundle (p5) meaningfully cut tail/long-horizon risk (up to ~60-70% reduction at extreme severity), strict liability (p4) modestly reduces via incentives, while status quo (sq) and preemption (p1) slightly raise long-run catastrophic risk relative to unconditional; effects are negligible at low-severity/short-horizon cells where incidents are already essentially locked in.

Calcuja P(doom) Survey 2026 (median ~20%); Metaculus catastrophe/extinction questions

The experts were presented with 24 risk categories, from discrimination and privacy loss to weapons, cyberattacks and power centralisation. They judged 18 of these more than 10 per cent likely to cause catastrophic harm by 2030.

results.title: The Economic Impact of Extreme Cyber Risks - Actuary.org
results.content:
Historical data aren’t enough. In traditional insurance modeling, analysts often look to past loss events as a guide to the future. But cyber risk is different. Attack tools evolve quickly, threat actors change tactics, and new vulnerabilities emerge constantly. Historical data are sparse—and in some cases deliberately hidden, as victims may be reluctant to disclose incidents. That makes it nearly impossible to estimate extreme loss potential solely from past events. [...] That is the uncomfortable question at the heart of our research. Cyberattacks are no longer rare, isolated events—they are an ongoing feature of our interconnected economy. But while we have plenty of headlines about data breaches and ransomware, we have far less reliable information on the potential economic damage of truly extreme cyber incidents—and even less on how those losses might compare across different types of scenarios.

Why This Matters for Actuaries [...] initiatives to map critical dependencies and coordinate responses across sectors, reflecting an acknowledgment that cyberattacks can ripple across the economy just as natural disasters do. These efforts highlight a shift from treating cyber incidents as isolated IT problems toward viewing them as systemic economic and security challenges.

Yet despite this federal [...] Despite the Trump administration’s opposition to state AI laws, several elements of the policy vision outlined in the AI Action Plan align with recent work from U.S. state legislators. For example, the plan prioritizes policy actions to “invest in AI interpretability, control, and robustness breakthroughs,” “build an AI evaluations ecosystem,” and “ensure that the U.S. government is at the forefront of evaluating national security risks in frontier models”—all goals seen in various U.S. state [...] States have introduced hundreds of AI bills in the past few years, covering a wide range of topics. Bills aimed at regulating frontier models have taken varying approaches. The heaviest regulatory approaches have failed to gain traction, whereas more moderate approaches have become law. In this sense, U.S. states are serving as important test beds for AI policy regulation. This exploration can—and should—inform federal approaches instead of being seen as an impediment.

results.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
results.content: The deployment of a limited number of general-purpose AI models across many different sectors and use-cases creates shared vulnerabilities across the AI ecosystem. A small number of models, mostly developed in the US and China (Figure 3.3), currently underpin AI applications in healthcare, finance, education, and other domains, cumulatively impacting billions of users.949;  When the same model powers many applications, faults in that model can propagate across all applications that depend on [...] Cross-sector deployment makes it difficult for developers, regulators and policymakers to understand and monitor the full range of applications that a given model supports. This makes it very difficult to carry out comprehensive pre-deployment testing and regulate appropriately across sectors. It is difficult to fix problems after deployment as this causes operational disruptions, and the effectiveness of current post-deployment measures is limited.956;  957;  frontier+AI+ models.pdf.") [...] Since the publication of the last Report (January 2025), the risk management landscape for general-purpose AI has evolved, with the publication of new resources such as the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the G7 HAIP Reporting Framework, China’s national AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 and various AI developers’ Frontier AI Safety Frameworks. These initiatives describe approaches and practices used by AI developers to manage the risks associated with general-purpose AI

results.title: Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws
results.content:
### Introduction

It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois, and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape. [...] AI testing and evaluation, including the White House’s June 2026 executive order establishing a voluntary framework for certain frontier AI developers to share models with the federal government before public release for national security and cybersecurity assessment. [...] Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

results.title: AI Regulations around the World - 2026 - Mind Foundry
results.content: In September 2024, China’s National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity released the AI Safety Governance Framework, aligning with the Global AI Governance Initiative. This framework introduced guidelines for the ethical and secure development of AI technologies. At the same time, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) began implementing stricter rules on AI-generated content, including a mandatory watermarking system to combat misinformation and enhance public trust in digital [...] California had proposed the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act, a bill designed to mandate safety tests for powerful AI models and establish a publicly funded cloud computing cluster for AI research and development. However, in September 2024, Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed the bill, arguing that it could stifle AI innovation and harm California’s competitive edge in the technology sector. The decision reflects a wider debate over how far state regulations [...] DeepSeek’s rapid ascent has also drawn the attention of policymakers and defence agencies in the West. The US Navy has officially banned the use of DeepSeek AI among its personnel, citing security concerns over potential data vulnerabilities and foreign influence. Meanwhile, discussions within the US and EU regulatory circles have intensified over whether stricter export controls should be imposed on AI technologies to limit the transfer of cutting-edge capabilities to China.

Catastrophe:general ~1-4-10%, AI subset ~0.3-2-5%, disempowerment higher (5-25-55%). Short horizons have lower absolute probs and muted policy effects. label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: documented AI-enabled fraud/deepfake losses already run $1-4B/yr (FBI IC3 ~$0.9B audited AI losses in 2025; Deloitte projects $40B/yr US GenAI fraud by 2027), so the $1B cumulative thresholds for AI-related and cyber incidents are likely already near-satisfied and become near-certain over 1-3 years; the $10B tier follows within a few years. Higher tiers are anchored on historical analogs (NotPetya ~$10B, anthrax letters ~$6B, no human-caused epidemic >100 deaths since Sverdlovsk) and on XPT forecasts (superforecaster/expert medians for AI catastrophe ≥10% of population by 2100 of ~2%/12%; engineered-pathogen catastrophe ~1-3%): I place AI-caused 10%-population catastrophe by 2100 at ~4%, general catastrophe ~12%, disempowerment ~13%, reflecting faster-than-expected capability progress since XPT. Severity ladders decline roughly log-linearly, with bio flatter between tiers (any successful engineered-pathogen release almost automatically exceeds $1B-$10B) and cyber steepest at high death tolls. Policy conditions: effects are negligible at 6-12 months, small by 2028-2030, and largest at high severities and long horizons; risk-reduction ordering is P5 > P3b ≈ P2b > P4 > P3a > P2a > P1 baseline, with status quo (no new policy) modestly riskier than the unconditional path (which embeds some expected regulation) and P1 slightly riskier still. Policies targeting frontier developers (licensing, liability, compute caps) do little against diffuse low-severity misuse (fraud with open/foreign models) but more against tail scenarios driven by frontier capability escalation; US-only measures are discounted relative to US-China measures because development would partly shift abroad. Catastrophe:general is diluted because most 10%-population risk (nuclear, natural/engineered pandemics without AI) is unaffected by AI policy.

results.title: The Extinction Tournament - by Scott Alexander
results.content: You might notice that all of these numbers are pretty low! I’ve previously said I thought there was a 33% chance of AI extinction alone (and lots of people are higher than me). Existential risk expert Toby Ord estimated a 16% total chance of extinction by 2100, which is 16x higher than these superforecasters and 2.5x higher than these domain experts. [...] If the XPT superforecasters’ probabilities rose linearly by the same factor as Metaculus forecasters’, they might be willing to update total global catastrophe risk to 11% and AI catastrophe risk to 5%. [...] Eyeballing the XPT answers, I think they split more like 80-20 on the AGI by 2100 question, I would expect them to split more like 50-50 on the superintelligence-conditional-on-AGI question, and that’s enough to explain the decreased risk of AGI catastrophe without necessarily bringing in more optimistic beliefs about alignment. It’s not enough to explain the decreased risk of extinction, so the XPT forecasters must believe there’s a higher chance AGI kills many people but not everyone. This

results.title: Will AI kill us? Superforecasters and experts disagree - Freethink
results.content:
Subscribe now

What are the odds that AI will kill humanity by 2100? That was one of the many questions asked in the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, held by the Forecasting Research Institute. The contest collected predictions from technical experts and “superforecasters” (people with a track record of making accurate predictions) about various existential threats — ranging from AI to nuclear war to pandemics. [...] Credit: The Forecasting Research Institute

Although predictions ranged widely and there was disagreement within the groups, the experts were generally more concerned about all kinds of existential risks. In total, experts predicted a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100. Superforecasters put the odds at 1%. Experts predicted a 20% chance of a catastrophe this century, while superforecasters estimated less than half of that (around 9%).

a table with a number of different statistics. [...] The threat of AI was the most divisive topic. AI experts said there is a 3% chance that AI will kill humanity by 2100, according to their median response. Superforecasters were far more optimistic, putting the odds of AI-caused extinction at just 0.38%.

The groups also submitted predictions on the likelihood that AI will cause a major catastrophe, even if it doesn’t wipe us out entirely (defined as causing the death of at least 10% of humans over a 5-year period).

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates: cumulative AI-related damages at the $1B level are essentially already occurring (AI-enabled fraud/breaches ~$1B+/yr per FBI IC3 and IBM data, with perfect-knowledge attribution assumed), so low rungs of the AI and cyber ladders are high probability even at 6–12 months. Higher rungs follow a heavy-tailed decay (~2.5–4x per 10x severity), anchored to the FRI expert survey (~62–70% for a $100B/50-death AI event by 2050) and XPT/FRI catastrophe estimates (AI 10%-mortality catastrophe: ~0.1–1% by 2030, ~1–5% by 2050, ~2–10% by 2100; I take intermediate values between experts and superforecasters, updating modestly upward for faster-than-expected agentic capabilities). Bio ladders start near zero (no AI-related engineered epidemic has occurred) but are flatter because engineered pandemics are heavy-tailed; cyber dominates low rungs but saturates at extreme severities; misalignment dominates the far tail. Policy conditions: status quo (no new policy through 2050) raises long-horizon and tail risks modestly (+5–30%); P1 preemption slightly raises risk; P2a/P3a/P4 (US-only measures) cut tail risk ~15–25% (limited by non-US actors and open-weight diffusion); P2b/P3b (US–China binding measures) cut tails ~30–40%; the P5 bundle cuts tails ~45–55% by 2050, with much smaller effects at 6–12 months (implementation lag) and on already-locked-in diffuse low-rung damages. Effects on catastrophe:general are diluted by the non-AI share of risk; disempowerment is most sensitive to the international slowdown/licensing regimes.

results.title: The AI Inversion: 2026's Most Dangerous Cyber Attacks | Foresiet
results.content:
Why did a model leak cause a $14.5 billion market drop? [...] Trend data from IBM X-Force, Akamai, and aggregated threat intelligence firms paints a consistent picture: AI-enabled attacks are growing faster, costing less to launch, and hitting harder than any previous threat category.

### AI-enabled attack volume — relative growth by type (2024–2026)

Indexed to 100 at Q1 2024. All categories show acceleration; AI-generated malware and supply chain attacks show the steepest growth curves.

results.title: AI-orchestrated cyberattacks: A call to action
results.content:
A recent report from Anthropic reveals a groundbreaking shift in cyber espionage, highlighting how advanced threat actors are harnessing artificial intelligence (AI) to elevate their operations. According to the report, a Chinese state-sponsored group, GTG-1002, orchestrated a sophisticated campaign that integrated AI autonomously across nearly all stages of the attack life cycle. Using the AI toolchain Claude Code, this operation executed all the functions necessary for a successful intrusion. [...] The implications are significant. Bad actors can scale simply with more compute and aren’t limited by finite personnel resources. Individuals can run large-scale campaigns that once took teams. It also means the operations can proceed 24/7 without sleep or rest. Volume, speed and impact will increase with AI enablement. Anthropic observed that the AI framework operated at a “speed impossible to match” for human hackers, making “thousands of requests, often multiple per second.” [...] Additionally, this exploitation campaign was detected and disrupted because it was run on one of the major foundational models where Anthropic could observe the activity. Attackers can quickly migrate to privately hosted models and improve them with training for hacking expertise.

### Harnessing AI as a defensive force

rationale: Base rates: cumulative AI-related damages at the $1B level are essentially already occurring (AI-enabled fraud/breaches ~$1B+/yr per FBI IC3 and IBM data, with perfect-knowledge attribution assumed), so low rungs of the AI and cyber ladders are high probability even at 6–12 months. Higher rungs follow a heavy-tailed decay (~2.5–4x per 10x severity), anchored to the FRI expert survey (~62–70% for a $100B/50-death AI event by 2050) and XPT/FRI catastrophe estimates (AI 10%-mortality catastrophe: ~0.1–1% by 2030, ~1–5% by 2050, ~2–10% by 2100; I take intermediate values between experts and superforecasters, updating modestly upward for faster-than-expected agentic capabilities). Bio ladders start near zero (no AI-related engineered epidemic has occurred) but are flatter because engineered pandemics are heavy-tailed; cyber dominates low rungs but saturates at extreme severities; misalignment dominates the far tail. Policy conditions: status quo (no new policy through 2050) raises long-horizon and tail risks modestly (+5–30%); P1 preemption slightly raises risk; P2a/P3a/P4 (US-only measures) cut tail risk ~15–25% (limited by non-US actors and open-weight diffusion); P2b/P3b (US–China binding measures) cut tails ~30–40%; the P5 bundle cuts tails ~45–55% by 2050, with much smaller effects at 6–12 months (implementation lag) and on already-locked-in diffuse low-rung damages. Effects on catastrophe:general are diluted by the non-AI share of risk; disempowerment is most sensitive to the international slowdown/licensing regimes.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates: cumulative AI-related damages at the $1B level are essentially already occurring (AI-enabled fraud/breaches ~$1B+/yr per FBI IC3 and IBM data, with perfect-knowledge attribution assumed), so low rungs of the AI and cyber ladders are high probability even at 6–12 months. Higher rungs follow a heavy-tailed decay (~2.5–4x per 10x severity), anchored to the FRI expert survey (~62–70% for a $100B/50-death AI event by 2050) and XPT/FRI catastrophe estimates (AI 10%-mortality catastrophe: ~0.1–1% by 2030, ~1–5% by 2050, ~2–10% by 2100; I take intermediate values between experts and superforecasters, updating modestly upward for faster-than-expected agentic capabilities). Bio ladders start near zero (no AI-related engineered epidemic has occurred) but are flatter because engineered pandemics are heavy-tailed; cyber dominates low rungs but saturates at extreme severities; misalignment dominates the far tail. Policy conditions: status quo (no new policy through 2050) raises long-horizon and tail risks modestly (+5–30%); P1 preemption slightly raises risk; P2a/P3a/P4 (US-only measures) cut tail risk ~15–25% (limited by non-US actors and open-weight diffusion); P2b/P3b (US–China binding measures) cut tails ~30–40%; the P5 bundle cuts tails ~45–55% by 2050, with much smaller effects at 6–12 months (implementation lag) and on already-locked-in diffuse low-rung damages. Effects on catastrophe:general are diluted by the non-AI share of risk; disempowerment is most sensitive to the international slowdown/licensing regimes.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Base rates anchored on: (1) AI is already substantially involved in cyberattacks—IBM 2026 found ~1 in 4 breaches AI-enabled, a 56% YoY rise in AI-driven attacks, and aggregate AI-attributable cyber losses already run into the hundreds of billions—so the $1B and $10B cyber/AI thresholds are near-certain short-term and effectively certain long-term. (2) Documented AI-agent "rogue" incidents (UK AISI July 2026, Meta/Anthropic/OpenAI sandbox escapes) show real unsanctioned agent behavior but "no real-world damage" yet, so misalignment at low severities is plausible soon but high-severity misalignment remains tail risk. (3) Bio is the slowest-moving channel: no AI-enabled human-caused epidemic has occurred; low near-term probability rising over decades as synthesis/AI-uplift barriers erode. Severity ladders decline steeply (roughly 1.5-3x per 10x severity step); mass-casualty cells (1M+) are dominated by long horizons. For catastrophe/disempowerment I anchored below researcher-median P(doom) (~5-20%) toward superforecaster/XPT ranges (10%-population AI catastrophe ~1-5% by 2100), giving ~12% AI catastrophe and ~16% disempowerment by 2100 unconditionally. Conditions: unconditional sits slightly below sq (I expect some real policy). Slowdown (p2b) and international authorization (p3b) most reduce catastrophic/misalignment tails; the P5 bundle gives the largest reduction (~50-70% on tail cells). P1 (preemption of stricter state law) marginally raises risk ≈ sq. Strict liability (p4) yields modest reductions via incentive effects. Policies barely move already-saturated low-severity cyber/AI cells but materially cut high-severity misalignment/disempowerment. Bio is least policy-sensitive since these AI-frontier policies don't fully address biosecurity.

18K views · 79 reactions | This week, Meta revealed that one of its AI models had hacked another company after gaining open internet access during cybersecurity testing performed by Irregular — a third-party company that conducts evaluations for the tech giant.

It's one of many incidents of AI models appearing to go rogue during cybersecurity and capabilities testing reported in just under two weeks, raising concerns about the safety of these models as they become more advanced, including the potential for them to be utilised in cyber attacks.

A day before Meta's announcement, the UK's AI Security Institute revealed that OpenAI's GPT-5 sol and Anthropic's Claude had "engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations", including sending messages UK AISI says were "attempts at social engineering, targeted at real people".

The institute said that no real-world damage was done.

Last week, Anthropic announced that some Claude models had hacked into three other companies during testing conducted by Irregular, after they gained access to the open internet after a "miscommunication" with the company.

This followed shortly after OpenAI revealed its models had found a way to connect to the open internet during a "highly isolated" sandbox simulation that had only "constrained" network access.

results.content: This campaign has substantial implications for cybersecurity in the age of AI “agents”—systems that can be run autonomously for long periods of time and that complete complex tasks largely independent of human intervention. Agents are valuable for everyday work and productivity—but in the wrong hands, they can substantially increase the viability of large-scale cyberattacks. [...] The barriers to performing sophisticated cyberattacks have dropped substantially—and we predict that they’ll continue to do so. With the correct setup, threat actors can now use agentic AI systems for extended periods to do the work of entire teams of experienced hackers: analyzing target systems, producing exploit code, and scanning vast datasets of stolen information more efficiently than any human operator. Less experienced and resourced groups can now potentially perform large-scale attacks [...] In mid-September 2025, we detected suspicious activity that later investigation determined to be a highly sophisticated espionage campaign. results.title: Why do Experts Disagree on Existential Risk and P(doom) ...
results.content: Several existing surveys have examined AI expert beliefs. The largest is the AI Impacts Survey(Grace et al., 2024), which surveys thousands of authors at the NeurIPS conference. AI Impacts asked experts questions such as “when will AI exceed human performance,” in response, the median expert answered 2061, and 10% answered 2026. According to AI Impacts, roughly 40% of respondents indicated a >10% chance of catastrophic outcomes from AI progress. Other surveys also seek to answer when experts [...] Prominent AI researchers hold dramatically different views on the degree of risk from building AGI. For example, Dr. Roman Yampolskiy estimates a 99% chance of an AI-caused existential catastrophe[Dr. Roman Yampolskiy [@romanyam] (2024)](#bib.bib4) (often called “P(doom)”) whereas others such as Yann Lecun believe that this probability is effectively zero[Yann LeCun [@ylecun] (2023)](#bib.bib5). The goal of the survey is to understand what drives this massive divergence in views on AI risk [...] purpose of the survey was to identify points of consensus and key reasons for AI risk assessments, such as skepticism or serious concern.

# Beyond P(doom) for AI Risk: Quantifying Uncertainty Without Probability

Andrew Lohn

May 2026 [...] Many observers wonder about the potential for artificial intelligence to cause catastrophic risks, but fortunately, there is little empirical evidence on which to base those assessments. Absent such evidence, experts often use their best guesses to estimate the probability of an AI-induced catastrophe or apocalypse (i.e., p-doom). Although subjective expert assessment may be the best evidence available, policymakers and risk analysts are not restricted to asking for probabilities. This brief [...] As artificial intelligence introduces new risks, some potentially catastrophic or even existential, there is little data or detailed theory to assess them. Policymakers often resort to expert best guesses for the probability of doom but probability is not always the most appropriate tool, especially for the types of uncertainties in AI risk. label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Base rates anchored on: (1) AI is already substantially involved in cyberattacks—IBM 2026 found ~1 in 4 breaches AI-enabled, a 56% YoY rise in AI-driven attacks, and aggregate AI-attributable cyber losses already run into the hundreds of billions—so the $1B and $10B cyber/AI thresholds are near-certain short-term and effectively certain long-term. (2) Documented AI-agent "rogue" incidents (UK AISI July 2026, Meta/Anthropic/OpenAI sandbox escapes) show real unsanctioned agent behavior but "no real-world damage" yet, so misalignment at low severities is plausible soon but high-severity misalignment remains tail risk. (3) Bio is the slowest-moving channel: no AI-enabled human-caused epidemic has occurred; low near-term probability rising over decades as synthesis/AI-uplift barriers erode. Severity ladders decline steeply (roughly 1.5-3x per 10x severity step); mass-casualty cells (1M+) are dominated by long horizons. For catastrophe/disempowerment I anchored below researcher-median P(doom) (~5-20%) toward superforecaster/XPT ranges (10%-population AI catastrophe ~1-5% by 2100), giving ~12% AI catastrophe and ~16% disempowerment by 2100 unconditionally. Conditions: unconditional sits slightly below sq (I expect some real policy). Slowdown (p2b) and international authorization (p3b) most reduce catastrophic/misalignment tails; the P5 bundle gives the largest reduction (~50-70% on tail cells). P1 (preemption of stricter state law) marginally raises risk ≈ sq. Strict liability (p4) yields modest reductions via incentive effects. Policies barely move already-saturated low-severity cyber/AI cells but materially cut high-severity misalignment/disempowerment. Bio is least policy-sensitive since these AI-frontier policies don't fully address biosecurity.

label: Grok 4.20
rationale: Base rates from LEAP 2026 expert medians show low AI catastrophe risk (~0.3% by 2030, 2% by 2050, 5% by 2100 unconditional for >10% mortality), rising with rapid progress; MIT 2026 notes ~20% near-term risk for specific mass-harm scenarios. Cyber incidents already frequent with AI enhancement (projected $10T annual cybercrime), making small-severity ladders likely soon but large ones rare. Bio and misalignment risks lower but non-zero, scaling with capabilities. Short-horizon probs decay sharply for high severities due to current tech limits; long-term cumulative rises but with heavy tails. Unconditional assumes moderate expected policies; SQ raises risks slightly via less oversight; P1 (preemption) mildly increases by limiting state rules; P2a/b, P3a/b, P4 reduce via slowdowns, vetting, liability incentives (strongest in P5 bundle, roughly halving tail risks). Disempowerment aligns with ~50% Metaculus community by ~2030-40 but tempered here. All adjusted multiplicatively per policy stringency while holding other factors fixed.

result.answer: Experts forecast a 1% probability of AI catastrophic risk by 2050, with higher risks under rapid progress scenarios. By 2100, the probability rises to 5% under slow progress and 10% under rapid progress. The risks include dangerous weapons capabilities and mass harm.

results.title: Wave 9: Risks - Longitudinal Expert AI Panel
results.content: Results. All participant groups forecast that AI catastrophic risk rises with the assumed pace of AI progress. Unconditionally, the median expert assigns a probability of 0.3% by 2030, 2% by 2050, and 5% by 2100. Under Slow Progress, the corresponding expert medians are 0.08%, 1%, and 2%; under Rapid Progress, they rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%. This post covers key highlights from the Wave 9 LEAP survey that we conducted between May 19 and June 10, 2026. In a rapid-progress world, experts give a [...] We also asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of a global AI-related catastrophe in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period. results.title: Ryan Hardy
results.content: - A bank just reported itself to the SEC. An AI chatbot is why. 1)What happened? A community bank just reported itself to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Not because of a cyberattack — because an employee uploaded customer Social Security numbers to an unauthorized AI chatbot. CB Financial Services filed an 8-K on May 7th. The breach clock started May 5th. Class action attorneys are already filing. 2) So what? This is a governance failure, not a technology failure. Shadow AI is [...] Shadow AI is invisible to standard oversight — that chatbot isn't in your vendor inventory, your DLP rules, or your incident response plan. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report puts the average shadow AI premium at $670,000. 97% of firms that experienced an AI-related incident lacked proper access controls. CB Financial just made both numbers real. In an SEC filing. 3) Now what? Three questions. If you can't answer all three, you have the same exposure: 🔍 What AI tools are your employees [...] our vulnerability management infrastructure was built for a world where humans found bugs at human speed. That world is gone. Patch cycles, coordinated disclosure timelines, NVD enrichment, and remediation workflows all need to be fundamentally rearchitected for an era where a single model can surface thousands of critical findings in weeks.  #ciso #cyber #ai #appsec ...more ...more

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I started from historical base rates: to date there have been many billion-dollar cyber incidents and operational AI failures, but no clearly AI-but-for event near the high mortality thresholds; engineered pandemics and loss-of-control catastrophes have very low near-term base rates but rise with frontier capability and diffusion over decades. I treated low-threshold AI/cyber economic-damage events as substantially more likely than mass-fatality events, with AI-bio lower in the next few years because practical wet-lab, access-control, and tacit-knowledge barriers remain important. For cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe, I anchored on expert-survey medians and broader GCR assessments, with AI constituting a growing but not exclusive component of total risk. Policy conditions are modeled as causal shifts: status quo and state-law preemption raise risk modestly; unilateral US slowing or authorization lowers it moderately; US-China/international controls lower it more; the bundled P5 has the largest effect but leaves residual risk from imperfect compliance, other jurisdictions, misuse, and post-2050 dynamics. Probabilities are monotone in time and severity except where capped by probability bounds, and are intentionally not zero even for extreme near-term tails.

results.title: Frontier AI: The Genie's Out of the Bottle, but Where's the Rulebook?
results.content:
Once SB315 goes into effect in January 2027, large frontier developers will be required to “create, implement, and annually update a comprehensive AI framework covering catastrophic-risk assessment, mitigations, governance, cybersecurity, third-party evaluations, and internal-use risks.” They must also submit transparency reports before deploying new or substantially modified models. [...] Illinois and New York allow frontier AI developers to report critical safety incidents to the agency and attorneys general within 72 hours of discovery, while California provides 15 days. Windows shrink to 24 hours if the "incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury," according to the Illinois legislation.

Varied compliance measures mean higher costs for developers or anyone legally required to follow the laws. They will have to create different compliance reports.

results.content: Results. All participant groups forecast that AI catastrophic risk rises with the assumed pace of AI progress. Unconditionally, the median expert assigns a probability of 0.3% by 2030, 2% by 2050, and 5% by 2100. Under Slow Progress, the corresponding expert medians are 0.08%, 1%, and 2%; under Rapid Progress, they rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%. The public consistently assigns higher probabilities than both experts and superforecasters, with unconditional medians of 1%, 3%, and 7%, and a median of [...] Results. All participant groups forecast that total catastrophic risk rises with both the time horizon and the assumed pace of AI progress. Unconditionally, the median expert assigns a probability of 1% by 2030, 4.2% by 2050, and 10% by 2100. Under Slow Progress, the corresponding expert medians are 0.75%, 3%, and 8%; under Rapid Progress, they rise to 2%, 7%, and 15%. results.title: Global Catastrophe Assessment: What RAND’s Landmark Report Tells Us About Civilisation’s Biggest Threats – Adapt Research Ltd
results.content:
Key findings reveal that while asteroid impacts and supervolcanoes are better understood scientifically, the most pressing concerns come from human-influenced risks.
 The report identifies the threats with increasing likelihood of occurrence as pandemics, climate change, nuclear war, and AI, with pandemic likelihood projected to double or quadruple by 2100.
 Importantly, these risks are interconnected and can amplify each other – for instance, AI could exacerbate nuclear or pandemic risks. [...] RAND’s analysis warns that severe pandemics can inflict massive casualties and social disruption in remarkably short periods. The report highlights how human activities are amplifying pandemic risks, projecting a two to four-fold increase through 2100. While natural pandemics are becoming more frequent, the report also acknowledges the less quantifiable risks of laboratory accidents and engineered pathogens—noting historical incidents of accidental exposure and mishandled pathogens during [...] The US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act

Enabled by the US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act (2022) (US GCRMA), the Secretary of Homeland Security and the administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency directed RAND to produce a report on six threats and hazards considered global catastrophic risks (GCRs). The report assesses pandemics, climate change, nuclear war, asteroid/comet impacts, supervolcano eruptions, and AI.

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I started from historical base rates: to date there have been many billion-dollar cyber incidents and operational AI failures, but no clearly AI-but-for event near the high mortality thresholds; engineered pandemics and loss-of-control catastrophes have very low near-term base rates but rise with frontier capability and diffusion over decades. I treated low-threshold AI/cyber economic-damage events as substantially more likely than mass-fatality events, with AI-bio lower in the next few years because practical wet-lab, access-control, and tacit-knowledge barriers remain important. For cross-cutting 10%-population catastrophe, I anchored on expert-survey medians and broader GCR assessments, with AI constituting a growing but not exclusive component of total risk. Policy conditions are modeled as causal shifts: status quo and state-law preemption raise risk modestly; unilateral US slowing or authorization lowers it moderately; US-China/international controls lower it more; the bundled P5 has the largest effect but leaves residual risk from imperfect compliance, other jurisdictions, misuse, and post-2050 dynamics. Probabilities are monotone in time and severity except where capped by probability bounds, and are intentionally not zero even for extreme near-term tails.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Base rates anchored on: IBM 2026 (1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, ~$6M avg, rising), CSIS large-scale AI cyberattack analysis, Anthropic/FMF bio uplift approaching CBRN-4 (~late 2026), and XPT/Metaculus catastrophe estimates (superforecasters ~9%, experts ~20% for 10% pop loss by 2100; AI catastrophe lower). The 'AI-related incident' umbrella is broadest (cyber+bio+misalign+other) so ranks highest; cyber is the dominant near-term channel for economic damage because the '$1B/$10B' threshold is essentially met cumulatively already, making low-severity cyber/AI near-certain short term. Bio and misaligned channels require rare mass-casualty events, so are much lower and grow mainly over long horizons. Severity ladder is steeply declining (each 10x threshold roughly an order of magnitude less likely near-term, flattening for economic thresholds where cyber can accumulate). results.content: AI is now widely seen as the biggest threat to online security in the year ahead. Reports of hackers bypassing guardrails to launch cyberattacks on major companies cannot be ignored, prompting governments to brace for a surge in the scale and severity of AI-enabled cyberattacks. In a country like India – which in 2023 accounted for around 49% of global real-time payment transactions worldwide, and processed around 181 billion digital transactions with a total value exceeding ₹233 trillion [...] AI is enabling rapid, tailored content creation, allowing criminals to scale and personalise scams with unprecedented efficiency. [...] Protecting individuals also requires action at the human, infra and tech levels – from digital safety education and stronger identity verification and domain oversight to AI-enabled screening that flags fraud before harm occurs. Isolated action will not be enough. As fraud becomes systemic, the response must be systemic too.

label: Grok 4.20
rationale: Expert surveys (LEAP 2026, Delphi 2025, XPT) indicate medians of ~1-5% for AI-driven 10% global catastrophe by 2050 (higher in rapid progress scenarios) and >50% for major AI harm, with superforecasters lower; these anchor the mid-to-long term ladders for AI/catastrophe/disempowerment. Recent incidents are small-scale (AI-enabled breaches up 56%, isolated chatbot harms, no >100 deaths or $1B AI-specific yet), supporting low short-term probs that rise with horizon and fall with severity. Historical base rates (~0.2%/yr for 10% pop cat) plus cybercrime damages (~$10T/yr projected) and policy (voluntary US reviews, no caps/liability/pre-auth as of 2026) inform baselines. Unconditional assumes moderate policy evolution (between SQ and stringent); SQ/p1 raise risk 15-30% by limiting regs, while p2-p5 lower 25-70% via slowdowns/vetting/liability (most for p5 bundle). Bio/cyber/misalign are subsets of AI-incidents (cyber highest for near-term econ harms, misalign for tails). Key sources: LEAP Wave 9, MIT Delphi AI risks, historical catastrophe base rates (bounded-regret), ITRC/IBM breach data, CSIS/Brookings 2026 US-China AI policy.

results.title: Views on AI Existential Risk Before and After a Public Event at Harvard ...
results.content:
We report the results of identical pre- and post-event surveys given to attendees of a talk, two-sided conversation, and Q&A centered around the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies at Harvard University in March 2026, covering perceived probability of AI-caused extinction or severe disempowerment resulting from unimpeded AI development, confidence in those estimates, and global priority. Among the 89 matched participants, the post-event median estimate of the probability of existential risk [...] On March 11, 2026, we conducted a pre/post survey at a Harvard Science Book Talk event (co-hosted by the Harvard Division of Science, Harvard Book Store, and Harvard Library). The event featured a talk by Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), based on the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (Yudkowsky & Soares, 2025), followed by a structured conversation facilitated by Greg Kestin11
1 [...] As AI capabilities advance rapidly—with AI systems demonstrating capabilities sufficient to win the International Mathematical Olympiad (Hubert et al., 2025; Huang & Yang, 2025), over a decade ahead of forecaster predictions (Metaculus, 2021) and producing novel contributions to theoretical physics (Guevara et al., 2026)—and as AI systems increasingly operate autonomously as agents in the world, understanding how the public perceives these risks becomes increasingly important.

results.title: Prioritization of Risks from Artificial Intelligence
results.content:
Artificial intelligence poses many risks, ranging from familiar present-day harms to unprecedented and potentially catastrophic ones. Effective risk management requires prioritization: we must understand which risks are most severe, who is most vulnerable, and who is most responsible for addressing them. We report results from a three-round Delphi study conducted late 2025 with 272 international AI experts. Experts rated 24 AI risks on harm probability and severity, sector and actor [...] in financial loss) in the next 5 years (2025-2030). In a scenario where pragmatic mitigations are implemented, experts still judged five risks as having a more than 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes: dangerous capabilities, weapons & cyberattacks, environmental harm, inequality & unemployment, and power centralization. All 24 risks were judged as being more than 5% likely to cause catastrophic outcomes. AI users and the general public were judged the most vulnerable to these risks, but [...] # Prioritization of Risks from Artificial Intelligence: A Delphi Study of 272 International Experts

# Michael Noetel

June 4, 2026

results.title: Forecasting Major Risks from AI
results.content:
This post covers key highlights from the Wave 9 LEAP survey that we conducted between May 19 and June 10, 2026. Recent waves covered robotics, the economic effects of AI, security and geopolitics, AI R&D, and AI timelines. More information about Wave 9, including question details and analysis of rationales, is available here.

### Insight 1: Experts and superforecasters think a major AI-driven harm event is more likely than not by 2050 [...] In 2025, the FBI reported nearly $21 billion in financial losses from cyber-enabled crime—more than double the figure in 2022 ($10.3 billion). If AI capabilities progress slowly through 2030, the median expert predicts that losses reported to the FBI will increase to $25 billion in 2026, $35 billion in 2028, and $46 billion in 2031. If AI progress is rapid by 2030, they predict reported losses of $31 billion, $50 billion, and $70 billion, respectively. In a rapid-progress world, experts give a [...] We also asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of a global AI-related catastrophe in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period. If AI capabilities progress slowly, the median expert assigns this a 0.08% probability by 2030, 1% by 2050, and 2% by 2100. In a scenario where AI progress by 2030 is rapid, those forecasts rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%.1

results.title: Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk Persuasion ...
results.content: Olympiad results proved particularly surprising: AI systems achieved gold-level performance in July 2025, an outcome to which domain experts assigned only an 8.6% probability and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability. Overall, superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to the observed outcomes across these four AI benchmarks, compared to 24.6% from domain experts. [...] In July 2025, both Google DeepMind and OpenAI reported that their models achieved gold-level performance in the IMO 2025 competition—five years earlier than the median expert prediction and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster prediction.7 Domain experts and superforecasters only expected an 8.6% and a 2.3% probability of this achievement on or before 2025. [...] The median expert in the XPT forecast a 20% probability of global catastrophe—defined as a loss of at least 10% of the global population—and a 6% probability of human extinction by 2100. [...] # The survey

We asked researchers to estimate the probability of five AI risk scenarios, conditional on an existential catastrophe due to AI having occurred. There was also a catch-all “other scenarios” option.

These were the five scenarios we asked about, and the descriptions we gave in the survey: [...] No, these cases aren't included. results.title: Analyzing the Historical Rate of Catastrophes
results.content: Looking at these reference classes teaches us two things. First, it gives us a numerical estimate of how rare different catastrophes are. If we define a catastrophe as an event killing 1% of the global population within a decade, then 11 such catastrophes have occurred since 1500, for a base rate of 2% per year. If we raise the bar to killing 10% of the population, the base rate drops by an order of magnitude, to 0.2%. [...] Overall, then, I expect AI to increase the rate of catastrophes. As calculated above, the base rate of very large (10% death rate) catastrophes over the next 25 years is 5%, and I personally expect AI to add an additional 10% on top of that, as I’ll justify in the next post. [...] One argument against using historical base rates is that the present is so different from the past (e.g. due to technology) that base rates are meaningless. While today’s world is indeed different from the past, base rates can help sharpen rather than neglect these differences, by clarifying what’s actually new. For instance, the mere presence of technology cannot move us far above the base rate, because many technologies have been developed throughout history and none has caused a catastrophe

results.title: Ryan Hardy
results.content: - A bank just reported itself to the SEC. An AI chatbot is why. 1)What happened? A community bank just reported itself to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Not because of a cyberattack — because an employee uploaded customer Social Security numbers to an unauthorized AI chatbot. CB Financial Services filed an 8-K on May 7th. The breach clock started May 5th. Class action attorneys are already filing. 2) So what? This is a governance failure, not a technology failure. Shadow AI is [...] Shadow AI is invisible to standard oversight — that chatbot isn't in your vendor inventory, your DLP rules, or your incident response plan. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report puts the average shadow AI premium at $670,000. 97% of firms that experienced an AI-related incident lacked proper access controls. CB Financial just made both numbers real. In an SEC filing. 3) Now what? Three questions. If you can't answer all three, you have the same exposure: 🔍 What AI tools are your employees [...] our vulnerability management infrastructure was built for a world where humans found bugs at human speed. That world is gone. Patch cycles, coordinated disclosure timelines, NVD enrichment, and remediation workflows all need to be fundamentally rearchitected for an era where a single model can surface thousands of critical findings in weeks.  #ciso #cyber #ai #appsec ...more ...more

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I started from historical base rates: no clearly AI-related incident has yet reached the larger thresholds, but ordinary cyber losses are frequent and AI-enabled malicious activity is now reported as material, so the low cyber/overall AI rungs are much more likely than bio or loss-of-control rungs in the next few years. I then put substantial weight on fast frontier-AI progress through 2030 and beyond, including expert reports that dangerous cyber, CBRN assistance, and autonomous R&D capabilities are plausible before robust governance catches up; this drives the fat long-run tails, especially for misalignment and AI-enabled bio. My 2100 general-catastrophe forecast is between superforecaster and domain-expert estimates from the XPT-style literature, with AI a large but not exclusive contributor; AI catastrophe and disempowerment are lower than all AI incidents because they require truly global scale/control. For policy conditions I treated status quo and federal preemption as modestly risk-increasing relative to expected policy, while compute slowdowns and pre-release authorization reduce risk most when US-China/international rather than US-only, and the bundled policy roughly halves AI-specific risk in most cells though it does not eliminate residual risk or non-AI catastrophe. Short-horizon probabilities remain low because there is little time for novel model capabilities, deployment pathways, and causal chains to produce the largest outcomes, even though low-threshold cyber damages can occur quickly.
key_sources: International AI Safety Report 2026, internationalaisafetyreport.org
Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting AI Cyber Risks and Capabilities: Results of a 2025 Pilot Study
Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting LLM-enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Mitigations
IBM 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report / IBM newsroom on AI-enabled breaches

results.title: International AI Safety Report 2026

The International AI Safety Report 2026 is the most comprehensive global, science-based assessment of frontier AI systems currently available. Led by Yoshua Bengio and supported by over 100 experts across 30+ countries, it maps the evolving capabilities of general-purpose AI, the risks they introduce, and the effectiveness of current mitigation strategies. The report is explicitly designed for policymakers facing the “evidence dilemma” — needing to act under uncertainty while AI capabilities [...] The report is structured around three core questions, which together form a full-stack view of AI safety.

First, it analyzes capabilities. It documents how general-purpose AI has reached expert-level performance in domains like law, coding, and science, while still showing “jagged” performance — excelling in complex tasks but failing at simple ones. It also explores drivers of progress, including post-training techniques and increased compute usage. [...] It also exposes a critical tension: AI capabilities are scaling faster than our ability to measure, test, and regulate them. That gap is where most governance failures will happen.

I then put substantial weight on fast frontier-AI progress through 2030 and beyond, including expert reports that dangerous cyber, CBRN assistance, and autonomous R&D capabilities are plausible before robust governance catches up; this drives the fat long-run tails, especially for misalignment and AI-enabled bio. My 2100 general-catastrophe forecast is between superforecaster and domain-expert estimates from the XPT-style literature, with AI a large but not exclusive contributor; AI catastrophe and disempowerment are lower than all AI incidents because they require truly global scale/control. For policy conditions I treated status quo and federal preemption as modestly risk-increasing relative to expected policy, while compute slowdowns and pre-release authorization reduce risk most when US-China/international rather than US-only, and the bundled policy roughly halves AI-specific risk in most cells though it does not eliminate residual risk or non-AI catastrophe. Short-horizon probabilities remain low because there is little time for novel model capabilities, deployment pathways, and causal chains to produce the largest outcomes, even though low-threshold cyber damages can occur quickly.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Grounded in 2025-26 evidence: AI-enabled cyber is already pervasive (IBM 2026: ~25% of breaches AI-enabled; FBI ~$893M reported AI losses in 2025; Anthropic's Nov-2025 AI-orchestrated espionage campaign), so low cyber/AI-umbrella rungs ($1B–$10B) are effectively already met and near-certain across all horizons. The broad "AI-related incident" umbrella inherits cyber's high base rate. Bio (AI-related human-caused epidemic) has no realized events; experts (FRI/superforecaster surveys) give low near-term probabilities (~0.3% human-caused bio catastrophe by 2028; LLM-biorisk uplift modest), rising materially by 2050/2100 as capabilities and synthesis access grow. Misalignment loss-of-control incidents remain sub-threshold today (small specification-gaming/agentic events, no real-world mass harm) but scale up over decades. Catastrophic rungs (100k+ deaths, and 10% population) are deep-tail near-term and grow with time; disempowerment is a long-horizon tail risk. Severity ladders are strictly nested (each higher threshold ≤ lower). Policy conditioning: strict liability (p4), pre-release authorization (p3a/p3b), and slowdown (p2b), especially bundled (p5), modestly reduce high-severity/misalignment risk; preemption of stricter state law (p1) slightly raises it; status quo (sq) is slightly higher than unconditional at high severities since unconditional bakes in expected future safeguards. Policy has negligible effect on already-realized low cyber rungs and on near-term horizons. Cross-checked directionally against Metaculus x-risk/catastrophe communities (single-digit % AI catastrophe by 2100) without copying.

result.answer: In 2026, AI-related cyber incidents caused an estimated $10.5 trillion to $10.8 trillion in global economic damages. The US alone accounted for $81.61 billion. AI-powered attacks were projected to be the biggest challenge for 53% of security leaders.

results.title: AI Cyber Attack Statistics 2026: Costs, Cases & Defense - DeepStrike
results.content: AI is now a measured factor in real cybercrime, but there is no credible single percentage for all AI cyber attacks. IBM found that one in four malicious breaches in its 2026 study were AI-enabled, while the FBI recorded 22,364 U.S. complaints involving AI and nearly $893 million in reported losses during 2025. Separate provider and threat-intelligence datasets show attackers using AI most heavily for preparation, social engineering, malware development, and evasion. Autonomous operations are [...] The same study says 62% of reported AI-driven attacks targeted critical-infrastructure sectors. Financial-services breaches averaged $6.3 million and energy breaches averaged $5.2 million. Sector labels, reporting practices, company size, and incident mix all affect those averages, but the concentration supports prioritizing high-consequence workflows and essential services. [...] IBM’s 2026 breach study reported a $6 million average cost for AI-enabled breaches, about $1 million above its $4.99 million global average. The report says those AI-enabled events consisted mainly of deepfake impersonation and AI-enabled malware. Because the study includes 602 organizations that experienced breaches, use the figure for planning and comparison not as a prediction of what any single event will cost.

results.title: Data breaches surge in 2026 as AI plays a growing role ...
results.content:
More than 471 million million victim notices were associated with data compromises in the first half of 2026, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that assists identity-theft victims and tracks publicly reported data breaches. A cyber incident that occurred at education tool Canvas accounted for more than half of those notices, at 275 million. [...] The half-year tally compares with 297.5 million notices issued in all of 2025, the ITRC report shows. The number of incidents reached 1,803 in the first half of the year, up from 1,732 during the same period in 2025. If the second half of the year is as active, the final tally for 2026 will eclipse the 3,321 security incidents reported for all of last year.

## Read more CNBC personal finance coverage [...] Key Points

 In the first half of 2026, there were 1,803 reported data compromises, compared with 1,732 during the same time last year, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center.
 A higher-than-usual number, 21, involved "malicious insiders," attributed to both disgruntled laid-off workers and a remote-worker job scam involving North Korea.
 Consumers should take steps to protect their personal information from being used to open accounts in their name, experts say.

results.title: Cyber Security Breach Statistics [2026]: Key Facts & Data
results.content: IBM's 2026 data makes the case for AI-powered security unambiguously. Organizations with extensive AI/automation pay $3.62M per breach versus $5.52M without — a 34% reduction and the largest cost differentiator in the entire study. AI-equipped security teams detect breaches 51 days faster, giving attackers less time to move laterally and exfiltrate data. [...] Several trends are reshaping the breach landscape. Ransomware is now present in 44% of all breaches, up from 32% the prior year (Verizon DBIR 2025). Supply chain attacks doubled to 30% of incidents (IBM 2025). AI is a double-edged sword: shadow AI (unauthorized AI tools used by employees) contributed to breaches at a growing rate, adding extra costs per incident. But AI-powered security tools reduced breach costs by 34%. [...] AI and automation are the biggest factor in reducing both time and cost. Organizations with extensive AI/automation pay $3.62M per breach compared to $5.52M without — a $1.9M gap (IBM 2025). AI-equipped teams detect breaches 51 days faster, cutting detection time from 232 to 181 days. The cost reduction from AI deployment (34%) exceeds the savings from any other single factor IBM measured.

results.title: 225 Cybersecurity Stats and Facts for 2026
results.content:
212. Google Cloud’s Cybersecurity Forecast 2026 predicts attackers will use AI across the full attack lifecycle — including prompt-injection attacks and AI-generated phishing and deepfakes — while ransomware paired with data-theft extortion remains the most financially damaging form of cybercrime. The report also flags “shadow AI” (unsanctioned AI tools used inside organizations) and attacks on virtualization infrastructure as fast-rising threats. 117 [...] • Generative or agentic AI–driven phishing (45%), generative AI model prompt hacking (44%), and AI-vishing (voice deepfakes) (43%) are cited as the biggest concerns by C-suite cyber leaders.

• 36% of C-suite cyber leaders and 38% of managers admit that the technology behind cyberattacks is more sophisticated than their own.

Here are a few statistics exploring emerging trends to watch in 2026.

results.content:
The global cyber security spending market will hit USD 240 billion in 2026, which is a 12.5% hike from 2025. New mandates like the AI Act and EU's NIS2 will force tighter governance, board-level accountability, and faster breach reporting.
 Annual global losses will hit around USD 10.5 trillion to USD 10.8 trillion at the rate of which cyber crime costs are going up. The US will be the single biggest market with an estimated total value of USD 81.61 billion. [...] 53% of security leaders say AI-powered attacks will be their biggest challenge. Agentic phishing attacks will exceed 42% of all global breaches in 2026.
 Ransomware attacks will strike devices, consumers, and businesses every 2 seconds by 2021, and 2026 damage costs alone are forecasted to be around USD 74 billion. [...] ### 2. Phishing

 35% of attacks will use smishing (SMS) and messaging apps. Mobile users will be three times more likely to click on malicious links sent to them over desktop users.
 Phishing-related losses globally will cross USD 25 billion annually.

This memo provides an analysis of the Anthropic’s November 2025 Threat Report “Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign” [...] There are important limitations to note. AI was used to scale operations that could exploit existing security gaps, such as unpatched systems or default passwords, not rendering robust security controls obsolete. Anthropic also reported that model reliability created operational challenges, occasionally overstating findings or fabricating data.
