Recent reporting from BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, and HackRead Media reveals that threat actors, including Chinese state-aligned groups, have successfully jailbroken Anthropic’s Claude to bypass safety controls and generate malicious output such as exploit code, [...] The AI firm Anthropic says it discovered a major cyber campaign in September 2025, in which a high-confidence Chinese state-sponsored group used its AI model (Claude / Claude Code) to automate nearly the entire attack lifecycle—reconnaissance, exploit generation, credential harvesting, data exfiltration.    👉 What Happened: The group targeted about 30 global organisations (tech firms, financial institutions, chemical manufacturers, government agencies).  Around 80-90% of the campaign tasks [...] AI Just Pulled Off a Major Cyberattack. In September 2025, something unprecedented happened: an AI system carried out a large-scale cyberattack against global companies and government agencies with minimal human involvement. This wasn’t theory or science fiction. It happened, and it worked. Anthropic detected and stopped the operation, but what they uncovered is a wake-up call for everyone. What Actually Happened? results.title: Anthropic's AI-Run Attack and What It Means for Agentic Identity
results.content:
Anthropic called it “the first documented case of a large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention.” The campaign began in mid-September 2025, with the AI performing 80 to 90 percent of the operation. Humans stepped in at only four to six critical decision points per target while the agent maintained a pace no human operator could sustain.

## What the Attack Reveals About the Agentic AI Attack Surface [...] The OWASP Agentic Top 10, released in December 2025, ranks identity and privilege abuse (ASI03) and agent goal hijacking (ASI01) among its top risks precisely because agents amplify the consequences of every over-permissioned credential and every missing access boundary. [...] ## From Incident to Architecture

Anthropic’s disclosure is the clearest signal yet that the agentic AI attack surface demands dedicated security architecture. The discussion since November 2025 has focused on the rise of nonhuman actors inside enterprise environments and the need for tighter oversight. Those points are valid but tend to stay high level.

results.content: We report the results of identical pre- and post-event surveys given to attendees of a talk, two-sided conversation, and Q&A centered around the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies at Harvard University in March 2026, covering perceived probability of AI-caused extinction or severe disempowerment resulting from unimpeded AI development, confidence in those estimates, and global priority. Among the 89 matched participants, the post-event median estimate of the probability of existential risk [...] Probability of AI existential risk. “What probability do you put on future AI advances causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species? (Assume that companies developing AI technology proceed largely unimpeded by external intervention.)” The probabilities were separated into seven bins that served as answer choices: Under 5% (very unlikely or impossible), 5–20% (unlikely), 20–40% (possible but unlikely), 40–60% (roughly a coin flip), 60–80% (more [...] Overall, self-reported probability of AI existential risk increased significantly following the event (Wilcoxon signed-rank W=73W=73, p<0.001p<0.001, one-sided; likelihood ratio 3,734:13{,}734{:}1), with a mean shift of +6+6 percentage points across all 89 matched participants. Of the 35 participants whose responses changed, 29 shifted upward and 6 shifted downward.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Grounded in 2025-26 evidence: AI-enabled cyber is already pervasive (IBM 2026: ~25% of breaches AI-enabled; FBI ~$893M reported AI losses in 2025; Anthropic's Nov-2025 AI-orchestrated espionage campaign), so low cyber/AI-umbrella rungs ($1B–$10B) are effectively already met and near-certain across all horizons. The broad "AI-related incident" umbrella inherits cyber's high base rate. Bio (AI-related human-caused epidemic) has no realized events; experts (FRI/superforecaster surveys) give low near-term probabilities (~0.3% human-caused bio catastrophe by 2028; LLM-biorisk uplift modest), rising materially by 2050/2100 as capabilities and synthesis access grow. Misalignment loss-of-control incidents remain sub-threshold today (small specification-gaming/agentic events, no real-world mass harm) but scale up over decades. Catastrophic rungs (100k+ deaths, and 10% population) are deep-tail near-term and grow with time; disempowerment is a long-horizon tail risk. Severity ladders are strictly nested (each higher threshold ≤ lower). Policy conditioning: strict liability (p4), pre-release authorization (p3a/p3b), and slowdown (p2b), especially bundled (p5), modestly reduce high-severity/misalignment risk; preemption of stricter state law (p1) slightly raises it; status quo (sq) is slightly higher than unconditional at high severities since unconditional bakes in expected future safeguards. Policy has negligible effect on already-realized low cyber rungs and on near-term horizons. Cross-checked directionally against Metaculus x-risk/catastrophe communities (single-digit % AI catastrophe by 2100) without copying.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: AI-related economic harms at the $1B cumulative level are essentially already occurring (deepfake/AI-enabled fraud >$1.5B in 2025 alone, FBI logged ~$893M AI-crime losses, Anthropic documented the first largely-autonomous AI-orchestrated cyberattack, and 2026 brought multiple AI agent containment failures), so low rungs of the general-AI and cyber ladders are high probability even at 6–12 months, while no AI-related human-caused epidemic has ever occurred, keeping the bio ladder low near-term but rising with capability diffusion. I assumed roughly order-of-magnitude decay per severity rung, flattening at the tail (heavy-tailed damage distributions), with the general AI ladder ≥ the union of the cyber, bio, and misalignment sub-ladders plus other channels (autonomous weapons, AI-enabled escalation). Tail estimates (100M–1B deaths, 10%-population catastrophe, disempowerment) are anchored to expert surveys and Metaculus Ragnarök-type figures (AI-driven 10% population loss by 2100 ~2–10%; I use ~8% for catastrophe:ai, ~15% for any catastrophe, ~30% for the broad disempowerment definition which includes soft/implicit loss of control). Policy conditions are modeled as multipliers that are near-1 for short horizons and low severities (harms already in motion, driven by widely diffused non-frontier models) and largest for high severities and long horizons: status quo and federal preemption modestly raise tail risk (+5–20%); a US-only compute cap or US federal licensing cuts tail risk ~10–20% (limited by offshore/open-weight development); US–China slowdown or international licensing cuts tails ~25–45%; strict liability cuts mid-severity deployed-model harms ~10–15% but less at uninsurable extremes; the P5 bundle is strongest (~45–55% tail reduction by 2050, fading somewhat by 2100 since the measures lapse in 2050). Misalignment rungs get slightly stronger policy sensitivity (pre-release authorization and liability directly target loss-of-control), while bio/cyber misuse is less policy-elastic. Catastrophe:general blends AI-share (~25% of that risk by 2030, ~45% later) so policy effects are diluted.

results.title: AI Cyber Attack Statistics 2026: Costs, Cases & Defense
results.content:
Anthropic described the event as the first documented large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention. It estimated that AI performed 80%–90% of campaign work, with human decisions at a small number of critical points. This is a provider-authored incident assessment based on visibility into its own service; independent public validation is limited. [...] Agentic tools can plan subtasks, invoke tools, interpret results, and continue with limited supervision. That creates a genuine speed and scale concern, yet current evidence does not support calling most attacks autonomous. Anthropic observed AI use for lateral movement in 54 of 832 sampled malicious accounts, or 6.5%, and for privilege escalation and impact stages in 22.5%. [...] Several scoped datasets point upward. IBM reported a 56% year-over-year increase in AI-enabled malicious breaches within its study, CrowdStrike reported an 89% increase in attacks by AI-enabled adversaries in its visibility, and Anthropic’s medium-or-higher risk share rose between halves of its selected sample. These are consistent directional signals, not a universal growth rate.

results.title: Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 - Alignment Science Blog
results.content: As AI agents become more capable, widely deployed, and integrated into economically useful tasks, developers are giving them more tools and permissions to make decisions without human input. We can already see this autonomy in real deployments such as Project Vend,1 where an AI agent runs a profitable in-office shop, and OpenClaw, a harness that equips agents with broad permissions and tools for personal use. In some cases, this degree of autonomy comes with negative consequences: models can [...] 1. Project Vend is Anthropic’s experiment, run with Andon Labs, in which a Claude instance nicknamed “Claudius” was given autonomous control of a small in-office shop. The first phase lost money and Anthropic judged it a failure, but the shop turned a profit in the second phase after the team upgraded the model and added tools for inventory and customer tracking. Both phases produced incidents of bizarre behavior from the AI agent, such as Claudius claiming to be a human in a blue blazer and [...] models can engage in behaviors we have called “agentic misalignment”. The well-publicized MJ Rathbun incident provides a real-world warning sign: after a human maintainer of the matplotlib library rejected a PR from an autonomous OpenClaw agent, the OpenClaw agent published a personalized hit piece about the maintainer to coerce him into reversing the decision.

results.content: This incident is a clear example of AI misalignment, with AI systems pursuing objectives in ways their deployers never intended. In simple settings, misalignment can seem almost comical. For example, one AI model, tasked with preventing sorting errors in a list, realized that deleting the entire list guaranteed the absence of errors. But as AI systems become more capable of autonomously achieving complex goals, the same underlying problem can produce far more consequential behavior. [...] In the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, one of the models that went rogue was an unreleased internal model, more capable than anything OpenAI has deployed publicly. As of early 2026, the capabilities of internally deployed models were two months ahead of what was publicly available, a meaningful gap that will likely become even more significant as AI progress accelerates. But there is currently no government oversight over internal models’ capability levels, and thus no established channel for [...] Even worse, we may not know the full extent of misalignment incidents. Labs themselves may lack adequate monitoring to catch when their models are engaging in dangerous behavior or doing real harm. results.title: Ryan Hardy
results.content: - A bank just reported itself to the SEC. An AI chatbot is why. 1)What happened? A community bank just reported itself to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Not because of a cyberattack — because an employee uploaded customer Social Security numbers to an unauthorized AI chatbot. CB Financial Services filed an 8-K on May 7th. The breach clock started May 5th. Class action attorneys are already filing. 2) So what? This is a governance failure, not a technology failure. Shadow AI is [...] Shadow AI is invisible to standard oversight — that chatbot isn't in your vendor inventory, your DLP rules, or your incident response plan. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report puts the average shadow AI premium at $670,000. 97% of firms that experienced an AI-related incident lacked proper access controls. CB Financial just made both numbers real. In an SEC filing. 3) Now what? Three questions. If you can't answer all three, you have the same exposure: 🔍 What AI tools are your employees [...] our vulnerability management infrastructure was built for a world where humans found bugs at human speed. That world is gone. Patch cycles, coordinated disclosure timelines, NVD enrichment, and remediation workflows all need to be fundamentally rearchitected for an era where a single model can surface thousands of critical findings in weeks.  #ciso #cyber #ai #appsec ...more ...more

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: AI-enabled cybercrime already causes multi-billion-dollar cumulative annual losses (IBM 2026: 25% of breaches AI-enabled at ~$6M each; Deloitte: AI fraud ~$12-40B/yr), so the $1B and $10B cumulative rungs for cyber/AI-overall are near-certain to likely even within 6-12 months, while no misaligned-AI or AI-enabled-bio incident has yet reached even $1B, so those ladders start much lower and rise with agentic deployment and biotech uplift. Mid rungs are anchored on FRI's 2025 cyber pilot (5-8% for a single ≥$10B AI worm event in 2026) and GovAI damage modeling; extreme rungs are anchored on XPT (superforecasters: 0.38% AI extinction / ~2% AI catastrophe by 2100; domain experts 3.9-6% / 12%), adjusted upward because realized AI progress has repeatedly landed in the tails of superforecaster expectations. Policy conditions: I treat near-term horizons as nearly policy-invariant (implementation lag), with effects growing with horizon and severity — status quo raises mid/tail risk ~10-30%, P1 slightly raises it, P2a (US-only slowdown) is roughly neutral-to-mildly-protective given displacement to China, P3a and P4 cut deployment-driven and incentive-driven harms ~10-25%, P2b/P3b (US+China measures) cut frontier tail risk ~30-45% through 2050, and the P5 bundle cuts tails ~45-60% by 2050 with attenuation by 2100 (policies lapse in 2050). Cross-cutting questions are kept internally consistent: AI ladder ≈ union of sub-ladders, catastrophe:ai ≈ the ~1B-death AI rung, catastrophe:general adds non-AI risks (only its AI share responds to policy), and disempowerment reflects moderate probability of transformative AI with contested control by 2100.

result.answer: AI-enabled attacks caused billions in damages in 2026, with one in four breaches costing an average of $6 million. IBM reported a 56% increase in AI-enabled breaches compared to the previous year. AI-driven attacks are now faster, cheaper, and harder to attribute.

results.title: AI Cyber Attack Statistics 2026: Costs, Cases & Defense
results.content:
IBM’s 2026 breach study reported a $6 million average cost for AI-enabled breaches, about $1 million above its $4.99 million global average. The report says those AI-enabled events consisted mainly of deepfake impersonation and AI-enabled malware. Because the study includes 602 organizations that experienced breaches, use the figure for planning and comparison not as a prediction of what any single event will cost. [...] | 22,364 AI-related complaints and nearly $893 million in reported losses | U.S. complaint data | FBI IC3 complaints for 2025; not a global attack count and not limited to enterprise intrusions |
| 89% increase in attacks by AI-enabled adversaries | Vendor threat telemetry | CrowdStrike intelligence for activity observed in 2025; not the share of every attack worldwide | [...] AI is now a measured factor in real cybercrime, but there is no credible single percentage for all AI cyber attacks. IBM found that one in four malicious breaches in its 2026 study were AI-enabled, while the FBI recorded 22,364 U.S. complaints involving AI and nearly $893 million in reported losses during 2025. According to the Metaculus community, the sooner we meet the criteria for a "general AI system," the higher the existential risk. The Metaculus and Manifold forecasters give an estimate of around 50% or [...] The AI also needs to be involved in the decisions leading to the disaster. Simply helping a human to, for instance, develop new weapons while not being involved in the decision making would not count.

There are similar questions on Metaculus, asking specifically about an AI malfunction causing loss of lives or economic damage before 2032: [...] First off, how likely does the Metaculus community think that an extreme disaster this century is? The question below operationalizes this with a straightforward criterion: “This question will resolve as Yes if the human population (on Earth, and possibly elsewhere) decreases by at least 10% in any period of 5 years or less.” This definition for ‘catastrophe’ or ‘extreme disaster’ is used for all questions in this section.

results.content:
In the XPT survey, for AI risk,the superforecaster  median estimates for extinction risk was 0.0001% for 2030, 0.03% for 2050, and 0.38% for 2100.

[...] Generally I would not recommend deferring to public opinion on difficult questions, but I think this is still worth keeping track of, as an indicator of how malleable people are to different question methodologies. Some of the trends seen in the general public will probably extend to experts and superforecasters as well.

In the XPT survey, for AI risk,the general public median estimates for extinction risk was 0.001% for 2030, 1% for 2050, and 2% for 2100. [...] The superforecasters rank nuclear risk as higher than AI risk up to 2050, but consider AI risk to be higher by 2100. This may be because at the time of the survey they were skeptical of short-term AGI, with only 20% believing that Nick Bostrom would declare AGI by 2050.

A similar pattern also emerged for AI-caused extinction: public survey participants gave a 2% probability, while superforecasters and domain experts gave forecasts an order of magnitude apart at the median: 0.38% and 3%, respectively. [...] 62 The domain expert and superforecaster forecasts in this table are the combined probability each group gave to the risk of extinction due to engineered pathogens and non-engineered pathogens in the post-XPT survey. See the “Biorisks” section below for more detail. results.title: Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk Persuasion ...
results.content: The median expert in the XPT forecast a 20% probability of global catastrophe—defined as a loss of at least 10% of the global population—and a 6% probability of human extinction by 2100. Superforecasters viewed the world as less risky, forecasting a 9% and 1% probability of global catastrophe and human extinction by 2100, respectively. This held across domains, though not uniformly: superforecasters and experts were much further apart on risk related to AI than on the risk of nuclear war. [...] Olympiad results proved particularly surprising: AI systems achieved gold-level performance in July 2025, an outcome to which domain experts assigned only an 8.6% probability and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability. Overall, superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to the observed outcomes across these four AI benchmarks, compared to 24.6% from domain experts. [...] In July 2025, both Google DeepMind and OpenAI reported that their models achieved gold-level performance in the IMO 2025 competition—five years earlier than the median expert prediction and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster prediction.7 Domain experts and superforecasters only expected an 8.6% and a 2.3% probability of this achievement on or before 2025.

results.title: What did forecasters get right and wrong in the largest existential risk ...
results.content: The results from the International Mathematical Olympiad were even more surprising: AI systems achieved gold-level performance in July 2025, an outcome to which superforecasters gave only 2.3% probability and domain experts 8.6%. Overall, superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to the observed AI progress outcomes across these four benchmarks, compared to 24.6% from domain experts.

# Global experts assess risk of AI catastrophes

5 June 2026

Person’s hands typing on a laptop keyboard with a digital overlay of a fluctuating line graph and waveform, surrounded by multiple red warning icons with exclamation marks, suggesting system alerts, data monitoring, or cybersecurity risks.

(Photo credit: InfiniteFlow / Adobe Stock. ) [...] Associate Professor Michael Noetel from UQ’s School of Psychology said the experts judged there to be at least a 10 per cent probability of catastrophic outcomes from AI over the next 5 years.  
  
“They assessed AI risk across 24 categories by answering 3 questions: which AI risks are most severe, who is most vulnerable to them, and who is most responsible for addressing them,” Dr Noetel said. [...] The research found that even if pragmatic mitigations were adopted over the next 5 years, 5 of the 24 risk categories were estimated more than 10 per cent likely to cause catastrophic outcomes.

Dr Neil Thompson, Director of MIT FutureTech, said the expert estimations were incredibly worrying.

"If we consider other mature areas of technology such as nuclear power or aviation, risks at that level would be treated as intolerable,” Dr Thompson said.

results.content:
In tort liability, there is precedent for attaching strict liability to dangerous activities or objects (such as keeping of certain animals, using or storing fireworks, or operating a nuclear power plant). An activity may be considered hazardous due to its unpredictability (such as the responses of a wild animal or the easily inflammable nature of fireworks) or due to its capacity to create catastrophic harm (fires, nuclear meltdowns). Both may be true for AI systems, as they are unpredictable [...] SB 53 mandates transparency reporting but limits these obligations to ‘frontier developers’ that develop ‘frontier models’ and limits the reporting to risks that are ‘catastrophic risks’. Catastrophic risk is defined as a single incident causing 50 deaths or more, or more than $1 billion in damages, in which an AI model is involved in (a) the development or release of a CBRN weapon, (b) conduct without meaningful human oversight that constitutes a cyber-attack or murder, assault, torture, or [...] Imposing non-contractual liability onto an actor generally requires multiple elements: a violation of a duty of care (not living up to ‘standard of care’) or some form of strict liability, causation (‘but for’ and reasonable foreseeability) and damage.

AI introduces several challenges that impact on one or more of these elements and make it harder for claimants to effectively sue for compensation through liability. The examples below indicate some of these challenges.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I base my forecasts on the current trajectory of AI capabilities, historical base rates for catastrophic events, and the expected impact of various policy interventions. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the risk is dominated by existing models and conventional cyber/bio vulnerabilities, so policies have minimal effect. For medium to long-term horizons (2028-2100), the risk scales significantly as AI capabilities approach and exceed human level. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for economic damages, while bio and misaligned AI pose the greatest existential risks. Policies that slow down frontier R&D globally (p2b) or impose strict liability (p4) and pre-release authorization (p3b) significantly reduce tail risks. The bundle policy (p5) provides the strongest mitigation, reducing catastrophic risks by up to 70% in the long run. Conversely, federal preemption (p1) slightly increases risk by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal action.

results.content: - A bank just reported itself to the SEC. An AI chatbot is why. 1)What happened? A community bank just reported itself to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Not because of a cyberattack — because an employee uploaded customer Social Security numbers to an unauthorized AI chatbot. CB Financial Services filed an 8-K on May 7th. The breach clock started May 5th. Class action attorneys are already filing. 2) So what? This is a governance failure, not a technology failure. Shadow AI is [...] Shadow AI is invisible to standard oversight — that chatbot isn't in your vendor inventory, your DLP rules, or your incident response plan. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report puts the average shadow AI premium at $670,000. 97% of firms that experienced an AI-related incident lacked proper access controls. CB Financial just made both numbers real. In an SEC filing. 3) Now what? Three questions.
